ranges.en: A sukkah higher than twenty cubits is invalid.
Rabbi Judah dissents and validates a sukkah higher than twenty cubits.
A sukkah under ten handbreadths, lacking three walls, or with more shade than sun is invalid.
The Gemara cites an alley crossbeam mishnah where Rabbi Judah says lowering the beam is unnecessary.
Why does the sukkah rule declare invalidity while the alley rule instead provides a remedy?
A sukkah rule is Torah-based, so it is declared invalid; the alley rule is rabbinic, so a remedy applies.
Alternatively, even Torah-based rules allow remedies; the sukkah rule is stated briefly because it has many conditions.
Asks from where the height limit is known.
Rabbah introduces his answer.
Cites Leviticus 23:43 about the Israelites dwelling in sukkot as the source.
Explains that up to twenty cubits one knows he dwells in a sukkah, but higher he cannot see it.
Rabbi Zera introduces his own scriptural source for the height limit.
Cites Isaiah 4:6 about a sukkah providing shade by day.
Up to twenty cubits one sits in the sukkah's shade; higher, only the walls provide shade.
Abaye objects: a sukkah made under Ashteroth Karnayim above twenty cubits would also be invalid.
Reply: Ashteroth Karnayim do provide shade, whereas without walls there is no sukkah shade.
Rava answers and introduces his scriptural source.
Cites Leviticus 23:42 about dwelling in sukkot for seven days.
The Torah requires leaving permanent housing and dwelling in temporary housing during the festival.
Up to twenty cubits one makes a temporary home; above twenty cubits the home must be permanent, not temporary.
Abaye objects: a sukkah with iron walls and skhakh above would also be invalid.
Rava clarifies his position: he means that a rule applies only up to twenty cubits.
Up to twenty cubits, a temporary home made permanent still fulfils the obligation.
Above twenty cubits, a permanent home made temporary does not fulfil the obligation.

ranges.en: Rejects Rabbah's view as mere generational knowledge rather than a ruling to follow.
Rejects Rabbi Zeira's view because the verse he relies on refers to the messianic era.
Challenges Rabbi Zeira: if his reading were right, the verse should have said canopy instead of sukkah.
Asks what the word sukkah then adds, quoting the verse.
Concludes that the verse teaches both points.
Rejects Rava's view because of an objection raised by Abaye.
Asks whose opinion the following statement follows.
Reports Yoshia in Rav's name: dispute only when walls do not reach the covering; otherwise valid above twenty cubits.
The ruling follows Rabbah's reasoning: the eye cannot detect the sukkah above twenty cubits, but walls reaching the covering make it detectable.
Asks whose opinion the following statement of Rav Huna follows.
Reports Rav Huna in Rav's name: dispute only when the sukkah is four by four cubits; larger ones are valid even above twenty cubits.
Attributes this to Rabbi Zeira's shade rationale, since a spacious sukkah provides shade.
Asks whose opinion the next statement follows.
Reports Rav Chanan bar Rabbah in Rav's name: dispute only when the sukkah holds a head, body-majority and table; larger ones are valid above twenty cubits.
Resolves the question: the ruling follows no single authority.
Explains why Rabbi Yoshia can disagree with Rav Huna and Rav Chanan: they set a minimum size while he does not.
Proposes that Rav Huna and Rav Chanan disagree about the minimum size itself, rather than about the principle.
Rejects the proposal: both agree on the head-body-table minimum, and the disagreement lies elsewhere.
Explains the other side's position: the dispute concerns sizes between head-body-table and four cubits square.
Raises a baraita objection: a sukkah above twenty cubits is invalid, yet Rabbi Yehuda validates it up to forty or fifty cubits.
Rabbi Yehuda cites the anecdote of Queen Heloni in Lud, whose high sukkah elders entered without objection.
The Sages object that this is no proof, since the queen was a woman exempt from the sukkah mitzvah.
Rabbi Yehuda replies that she had seven sons and that she acted only on the Sages' instruction.
Asks why the reply needs the added clause that she acted only on the Sages' instruction.
Explains the added clause: if the sons were minors, one must have been old enough to be independent, and educating him is only rabbinic.
Concludes the argument and introduces a supporting baraita.
Cites the baraita stating that the queen did nothing except on the Sages' instruction.
Explains the baraita on the view that the dispute concerns sukkot whose walls do not reach the covering, as the queen's custom suggests.

ranges.en: Explains the queen's choice of a sukkah by reference to ventilation rather than a sitting requirement.
Describes the position that the Bais Shammai and Bais Hillel dispute concerns only a small sukkah.
Asks whether a queen customarily sits in a small sukkah, which would undercut the position just stated.
Rabbah bar Rav Adda replies that the ruling applies only to a sukkah with many recesses.
Asks again whether a queen customarily sits in a sukkah with many recesses.
Rav Ashi replies that the ruling concerns only the recesses within such a sukkah.
The Rabbis hold that the sons sat in the proper sukkah while the queen sat in a recess out of modesty.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that the sons sat with her, yet still no one remarked on it.
Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak rules that a sukkah must contain the head, most of the body, and the table.
Rabbi Abba asks whether this ruling follows Bais Shammai.
Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak replies that the ruling follows no one else.
Rabbi Abba asks who holds this opinion.
Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak answers that it is Bais Shammai's view and must not be changed.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that the dispute may concern a large sukkah with the table inside the house.
Supports the objection from the Mishnah's wording, which would otherwise have been phrased as contain or not contain.
Objects that the schools do not dispute a small sukkah, citing a baraita that a head, body and table suffice.
Cites Rabbi's baraita requiring a sukkah of four by four cubits.
Cites a second baraita: Rabbi invalidates a sukkah not four by four, while the Sages validate one holding the head and body.
Notes the two baraitas contradict each other unless one is from Bais Shammai and one from Bais Hillel.
Resolves the contradiction by attributing one baraita to each school.
Mar Zutra cites the Mishnah's wording, which presents Bais Shammai and Bais Hillel as disagreeing on fulfilment.
Raises a difficulty about the wording of the Mishnah.
Resolves the difficulty: the schools dispute both small and large sukkot, and the text is defective and must be read differently.
Gives the corrected Mishnah text: the schools dispute a sukkah holding the head and body, with the table inside the house or absent.
Asks who the authority is for a baraita the Rabbis taught.
Cites the baraita listing the exemptions for a house not four by four cubits, from mezuzah to eruv.

ranges.en: Continues the baraita: a sukkah may not serve as a joint eruv between two cities, nor be divided by brothers or partners.
Asks whether the baraita follows Rabbi rather than the Rabbis.
Replies that the baraita can follow the Rabbis as well.
Explains that the Rabbis' limit applies only to a temporary sukkah; a permanent house with four cubits square is inhabited and counts as a dwelling.
Quotes the baraita: a sukkah is exempt from mezuzah, parapet, leprosy impurity, walled-city redemption, and return from war.
Asks for the reason for these exemptions.
Explains that the Torah's word house appears in all these commandments.
Continues the baraita: no eruv, shittuf, or eruv-placement is made in such a structure.
Asks for the reason the structure cannot receive an eruv.
Explains that it is unsuitable for habitation.
Baraita detail: a courtyard eruv cannot be placed in it, though a shittuf can.
Asks why the structure is no worse than a courtyard inside an alley.
Explains that it is no worse than a courtyard within an alley.
Cites a mishnah: courtyard eruvs are placed in the courtyard, and alley shittufs in the alley.
Raises an objection from a mishnah: an eruv placed in a gatehouse, exedra, or balcony should not be valid.
Resolves the objection by emending the text: courtyard eruvs go in a house within the courtyard.
Repeats the baraita that a sukkah may not serve as an extension between two cities.
Explains that such a structure is not even equal to a border outpost, since it serves no purpose.
Baraita: brothers or partners cannot divide it because it lacks four cubits square.
Infers that a structure of four cubits square could be divided.
Objects from a mishnah: a courtyard may not be divided unless each party gets four cubits.
Resolves the objection: the law of division does not apply to such a structure as it does to a courtyard.
Cites Rav Huna's ruling that a courtyard divides by its doors, and Rav Chisda's ruling of four cubits per door.
Limits those rulings to a house intended to stand, not a temporary hut meant for demolition.
Teaches that lowering a sukkah above twenty cubits by placing pillows and blankets inside does not count as lowering it.

ranges.en: Even when all the roofing is nullified, the owner's intention is nullified only with respect to himself, not others.
Straw that is nullified counts as lowering the roof, and earth that is nullified does so all the more.
Frames the dispute between Rabbi Yose and the Sages over straw or earth the owner does not intend to remove.
Cites a mishnah: a house filled with straw or stones is nullified only if the filler nullified them.
Cites a baraita of Rabbi Yose: intended-to-remove material is treated differently from material he does not plan to move.
Rules that a sukkah above twenty cubits is valid if palm fronds hanging within twenty cubits give more shade than sun.
Abaye proposes that a ten-handbreadth sukkah with fronds hanging inside is valid if sun is greater than shade.
Rava objects that such a sukkah would be a foul, uninhabitable dwelling, which a person would not live in.
Rules that a sukkah above twenty cubits with a platform along the middle wall is valid if it keeps the minimum area.
Asks what the rule is when the platform is attached from the side wall.
Rules that the side-attached platform is invalid if four cubits separate it from the opposite wall, and valid if less.
Asks what new point this ruling teaches.
Explains that the teaching confirms a curved wall counts as a wall, as already learned in a mishnah.
Cites a mishnah on a roofed house with a gap: invalid if four cubits from the wall, valid if less.
Explains the point: a mishnah on a suitable wall might be read as not applying to a wall that is not suitable.
Rules that a platform in the middle of a high sukkah is invalid if four cubits lie on every side, valid if less.
Asks what new point the ruling teaches.
Answers that the teaching again confirms a curved wall counts as a wall.
Asks what one might have thought.
Clarifies that the curved-wall rule applies to a single side, and the teaching extends it to every side.
Rules that a sukkah under ten handbreadths hollowed out to reach ten is invalid if the hollow's lip is three handbreadths from the wall.

ranges.en: A gap of less than three handbreadths in the roof leaves the sukkah valid.
Asks why the earlier case allows a gap of less than four cubits while this case is measured in handbreadths.
Asks the same contrast from the other direction, about the three-handbreadth standard.
Explains the difference: where a wall already exists, four cubits is enough; where a wall must be created, the gap must be under three handbreadths.
Presents a sukkah above twenty cubits with a ten-handbreadth pillar that could serve as a valid sukkah wall.
Abaye proposes that the partition can be drawn upward from the pillar to form a wall.
Rava objects: the partitions must be recognizable walls, and none exist here.
Teaching: Rabbi Yaakov validates a sukkah with skhakh over four poles driven into the ground; the Sages invalidate it.
Rav Huna rules that the dispute concerns poles at a roof's edge, where drawing the partition up applies; in mid-roof all agree it is invalid.
Rav Nachman holds the dispute extends to poles set in the middle of the roof.
The Gemara asks whether the dispute covers only mid-roof poles or both cases, and leaves the question undecided.
Objects with a baraita: skhakh over four poles in the ground is valid for Rabbi Yaakov and invalid for the Sages.
Argues the ground is like mid-roof, so the baraita refutes Rav Huna's position.
Adds a second refutation: the dispute is said to concern only mid-roof, so Rav Huna's view fails on two points.
Rav Huna can reply: the dispute covers both mid-roof and edge poles, and Rabbi Yaakov validates even mid-roof.
Teaching: Rabbi Yaakov counts the pillars as two-sided if a handbreadth remains after planing; the Sages require two proper walls.
Opens the next Mishnah: a sukkah under ten handbreadths high is invalid.
Asks how the Mishnah's ten-handbreadth height standard is known.
Cites a tradition from Rav, Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Chaviva as the source.
Parenthetical note on the transmission of the name Yohanan or Yonatan in Seder Moed.
The ark's nine handbreadths plus a one-handbreadth cover make ten; Exodus 25:22 is cited as support.

ranges.en: Baraita teaches that the Shechinah never descended to earth and Moses and Elijah never ascended to heaven.
Cites Psalms saying heaven belongs to God while earth was given to humanity.
Restates that the Shechinah never descended to earth.
Objects that Exodus describes God descending onto Mount Sinai, contradicting the claim.
Reply: that descent was above ten handbreadths, so it does not count as reaching earth.
Objects with Zechariah, where God's feet stand on the Mount of Olives, seemingly a descent.
Reply: that standing was also above ten handbreadths, so the view still holds.
Restates the baraita that Moses and Elijah never ascended to heaven.
Objects that Exodus says Moses went up to God, suggesting he ascended to heaven.
Reply: Moses ascended only to a point below ten handbreadths from heaven.
Objects that Elijah went up in a whirlwind into heaven.
Reply: Elijah rose only to a level below ten handbreadths from heaven.
Objects with Job, where God seizes the throne and spreads His cloud, implying a close approach.
R. Tanhum explains that God spread some of His Shechinah radiance and cloud onto the throne.
Reply: even this occurred at a point below ten handbreadths from heaven.
Objects that the verse says the face of the throne was seized, which seems to contradict the limit.
Reply: the throne was lowered until it was under ten handbreadths, and only then seized.
Concedes the ark was nine handbreadths tall, which the verse's dimensions indicate.
Cites Exodus 25:10 giving the ark's length, breadth and height in cubits.
Asks how we know the ark-cover was one handbreadth high.
R. Hanina's baraita: the Torah gave dimensions for every vessel except the ark-cover's height, so it must be deduced.
Deduces the cover's height from the table border, which is a handbreadth, by analogy from Exodus 25.
Objects: why not derive the measurement from the vessels themselves?
Reply: a derivation works only for the smaller measure, as a small amount is grasped but a large one is not.
Objects: why not derive from the golden headplate, which a baraita describes?
Baraita describes the headplate: a gold plate inscribed with Kodesh LaShem, seen in Rome.
Principle: a vessel's measurements may be derived from another vessel, but not from an ornament.
Objects: why not derive from the crown, whose measurements the Torah never gave?
Restates the principle: derive a vessel from a vessel, not from an accessory to a vessel.
Objects: by that logic the table border is also a vessel accessory, so its position matters.
Asks what can be said if the border was above the table, since it would then be a mere accessory.
Reply: derive measures only from items whose measurements the Torah gives, unlike the headplate or crown.
R. Huna proves the height from the face of the ark-cover, and a face is at least a handbreadth.
Objects: perhaps the verse's face means only a face-like surface, not a true measured face.

ranges.en: Repeats the reply that only a smaller measure can be grasped and used for deduction, not a large one.
Objects that the face may be like a very small tzipora, so the height is not a true face.
R. Aha b. Jacob reports R. Huna's view that the word face is learned by analogy between two verses.
Gezera shava: the word face appears in Exodus about the ark-cover and in Genesis about Isaac, linking them.
Objects: derive from the face above, as in Genesis 33:10 where Jacob sees God's face.
Repeats that deduction works only for the smaller measure, not the large one.
Objects: learn from the cherubim, whose faces are toward the ark-cover in Exodus 25:20.
Reply: a tradition holds that cherubim faces were no less than a handbreadth high.
Notes that R. Huna also derived the measure from this same verse.
Asks what a cherub is.
R. Abahu explains a cherub is like a child, since in Babylon children are called ravia.
Abaye objects: Ezekiel says the cherub face equals a human face, so the sizes cannot match.
Reply: the faces differ, one large and the other small, so the comparison is not exact.
Asks how we know the interior height is ten handbreadths, excluding the skhakh covering.
Rather, the measure is learned from the Temple, whose dimensions are given in Kings.
Cites Kings on the Temple's dimensions and the cherubim's height of ten cubits.
Baraita: cherubim stood at a third of the Temple's height, and likewise in the Tabernacle.
Asks how much ten cubits is, in order to calculate the Tabernacle's height.
Cites Exodus 26:16 that a board is ten cubits long.
Calculates that ten cubits is sixty handbreadths, and a third of that is twenty.
Deducts the ark and cover's ten handbreadths, leaving ten for the wings.
Cites Exodus 25:20 on the cherubim's wings and the Merciful One calling wings above ten a covering.
Asks how we know the wings were raised above their heads.
Objects: perhaps the wings were level with their heads instead.
R. Aha b. Jacob: the verse says on high, showing the wings were above the head.
Objects: perhaps the wings were raised extremely high, though the verse does not say on high twice.
Asks what can be said if R. Meir's normal cubits contrast with R. Judah's building and vessel cubits.
Calculates the ark and cover at eight and a half handbreadths, leaving eleven and a half.
Asks whether a sukkah must then be at least eleven and a half handbreadths high.
Rather, for R. Judah the law is a tradition given to Moses at Sinai: these measures are fixed halakhah.
Objects: minimal measures seem Torah-level, since Deuteronomy's list of produce is cited.
R. Hanin replies the whole verse was stated in allusion to the prescribed minimal measures.
Illustrates the wheat measure with a mishnah on the leprous house, where items become impure at once.

ranges.en: Mishnah continues: clothing stays clean until the time needed to eat wheat bread while reclining with condiment.
Illustrates the barley measure with a mishnah on bone-size impurity, which defiles by contact and carrying but not overshadowing.
Matches the vine verse to the quarter-log of wine forbidden to a Nazirite.
Matches the fig to the dried-fig size that counts for carrying out on Shabbat.
Matches the pomegranate to the size at which householders vessels can become impure.
Cites Deuteronomy 8:8 listing the land's produce, including olive oil and honey.
Explains the verse's land of olive oil as a land whose minimum measures are olive-sized.
Objects: it cannot mean all minimum measures, since some measures are not olive-sized.
Reply: rather, say the majority of its minimum measures are the bulk of an olive.
Matches honey to the date-size amount forbidden to eat on Yom Kippur.
Concludes that the minimum measures are therefore Torah-level law.
Asks whether measures are actually written in the Torah at all.
Reply: they are traditional halakhah, and the verse serves only as a support.
Objects: interposition is also Torah-level, since the verse requires nothing between the body and water.
Reply: the traditional law about hair is taught as Rabbah b. Bar Hana said.
Rabbah b. Bar Hana: one knotted hair interposes, three do not, but the status of two is unknown.
Objects: hair is also Torah-level, since the word et includes what is attached to the body.
Reply: the tradition is as R. Yitzchak stated.

ranges.en: Torah rule: hair interposes only if most of it is present and the person minds; the rabbis then decree on related cases.
Asks why the rabbis did not also decree on the minority-hair cases that are similar.
Reply: that rule is already a decree, and decreeing upon a decree is not warranted.
Asks: the partitions discussed above work for R. Judah, but what can be said for R. Meir?
Reply: the tradition covers the legal fictions of extension, lavud and the curved wall, and a sukkah lacking three walls.
Baraita: two walls must be full size and the third may be a handbreadth; R. Shimon requires three full walls.
Asks what principle the Tannaim disagree about.
The rabbis hold that tradition is authoritative, while R. Shimon holds that the written text is authoritative.
Counts the four references to sukkah in Leviticus 23:42 and deducts one for the law itself.
Following the rabbis, tradition reduces the third wall to a handbreadth, leaving two full walls.
R. Shimon's version: the word sukkot is read three times, so tradition reduces the fourth wall to a handbreadth.
Alternative resolution: all agree on the reading, but differ on whether the skhakh needs a Scriptural source.
Another resolution: all agree on tradition, but differ on whether tradition diminishes or adds to the measure.
Another resolution: they differ on whether one expounds first references in a verse.
R. Matanah gives R. Shimon's reason, citing Isaiah 4:6 on a sukkah providing shade and shelter.
Asks where the handbreadth of wall is placed.
Rav: place it opposite the departing wall.
Introduces R. Kahana and R. Assi addressing Rav, leading to a further objection against his placement.

ranges.en: Asks why the extra wall is not placed opposite the head of the diagonal wall; Rav remains silent.
Shmuel, in Levi's name, rules the extra wall is placed opposite the departing wall, as taught in the study hall.
R. Simon, or R. Joshua b. Levi, rules: make a loose handbreadth wall within three handbreadths of the wall, which counts as joined.
Rav Judah rules that a sukkah shaped like an open alley is valid, and the handbreadth wall may be placed on any side.
R. Simon, or R. Joshua b. Levi, rules: make a strip of about four handbreadths within three handbreadths of the wall.
Asks why one loose handbreadth suffices in the earlier case but a four-handbreadth strip is needed here.
Reply: with two valid walls a loose handbreadth suffices; without them, a four-handbreadth strip is required.
Rava rules it is valid only if the entrance has the form of a doorway.
Another version of Rava: a sukkah is valid even with the form of a doorway.
Another version of Rava: the form of a doorway is also required.
R. Ashi finds R. Kahana building a loose handbreadth wall together with a doorway form.
R. Ashi asks whether the Master holds Rava's view that the doorway form is valid as well.
R. Kahana: I follow the other version of Rava, which requires the doorway form in addition to the handbreadth.
Cites the rule that two walls must be of the prescribed dimensions.
Rava: the same applies to Shabbat, since a handbreadth counted as a wall for sukkah counts for Shabbat.
Abaye objects: do we really apply the rule of since, when a baraita says otherwise?
Baraita: sukkah walls follow the same rules as Shabbat walls, provided no gap of three handbreadths lies between reeds.
Baraita continues: Shabbat is stricter, since its wall must be solid enough to exceed its gaps, unlike a sukkah.
Asks whether this means Shabbat is stricter than sukkah, and whether the rule of since is not applied.
Reply: it means ordinary Shabbat is stricter than the Shabbat of a sukkah.
Objects: if so, the ordinary sukkah is stricter than a Shabbat sukkah, which needs no loose handbreadth wall.
Cites Rav's own ruling that a skhakh over an alleyway with a side-post is valid.
Reply: no need to state this, since the rule of since works in both directions.
Returning to the main subject, Rava said.

ranges.en: Skhakh placed over an alley that has a side-post is a valid sukkah.
Rava adds: skhakh placed over upright boards around wells is also valid.
Explains why the first case is needed: an alley has two proper walls, while well-boards do not.
Explains why the well-boards case is needed: it has four walls, unlike an alley lacking them.
Explains that the two cases together teach the rule of since in only one direction, so all three are needed.
Mishnah: a sukkah where the sun exceeds the shade is invalid.
Baraita: sun from lack of skhakh invalidates, but R. Yoshayah says sun from the walls also invalidates.
Attributes to Abaye, via Rav Yemar b. Shelamiah, the view behind R. Yoshayah's position.
Asks the reason for R. Yoshayah's ruling.
Cites Exodus 40:3 calling the veil a covering, so a partition must be as close as skhakh.
The rabbis: the veil is bent slightly at the top so it looks like a covering.
Abaye: all these authorities hold a sukkah must be built like a permanent dwelling.
Cites Rabbi's view that a sukkah less than four cubits square is invalid.
Notes that R. Yoshayah's view was already explained above.
Mishnah on R. Judah: a sukkah above twenty cubits is invalid, but R. Judah validates it.
Baraita: R. Shimon requires three walls of full size and a handbreadth for the fourth.
Baraita: R. Gamaliel invalidates a sukkah built on a wagon or ship, while R. Akiva validates it.
Mishnah: Beth Shammai invalidate a sukkah whose occupant's head is inside but table outside; Beth Hillel validate it.
Mishnah: R. Eliezer invalidates a sukkah lacking a roof, such as one leaning on a wall; the sages validate it.
Baraita: others say a sukkah shaped like a dovecote is invalid because it has no corners.
R. Yohanan: a round sukkah is valid if twenty-four people can sit around its circumference, otherwise invalid.
Asks according to whom R. Yohanan's ruling holds.
Reply: according to Rabbi, who requires a sukkah to be four cubits square.
Objects that a man occupies a cubit, so twelve men would suffice, which conflicts with R. Yohanan's measure.

ranges.en: The rule about the approximate sixteen-men figure applies only to a circle; a square needs a larger perimeter.
Asks: a square exceeds its inscribed circle by a quarter, so should sixteen men not suffice in a square?
Reply: the approximation holds for a circle inside a square, but a square inscribed in a circle needs more for its corners.
Asks: a square's diagonal gives about sixteen and four-fifths cubits, so should that not suffice, given the approximation?
Objects: approximating is tolerable for a small gap, but would it be assumed for a large one?
Mar Kashisha asks R. Ashi whether he thinks a man occupies one cubit of space.
Mar Kashisha's computation: three men in two cubits gives about sixteen cubits, so approximation is needed for the exact figure.
Objects: if approximation is allowed, does it apply in a lenient direction, or only where it makes the law stringent?
R. Assi: a man truly occupies a cubit, but R. Yohanan does not count the space the men occupy.
Calculating with eighteen cubits shows the approximation made the law stringent, not lenient.
The rabbis of Caesarea say the circumference of a circle inscribed in a square is a quarter of the square's.

ranges.en: Objects that the inscribed square is only half the circle, since the figures are not that different.
R. Levi in R. Meir's name: of two potters' sukkot, one inside the other, the inner is invalid and needs a mezuzah, the outer is valid.
Asks why the outer booth should not count as the gatehouse of the inner one, thus requiring a mezuzah.
Reply: neither booth is of a permanent nature, so the gatehouse analogy does not apply.
Mnemonic ganbak: sukkot of gentiles, women, cattle or Samaritans are valid if covered according to the rule.
R. Hisda: covered according to the rule means the covering was made to provide shade for the sukkah.
Asks what the phrase any sukkah whatsoever is meant to include.
Baraita mnemonic rakbash: sukkot of shepherds, fig-pickers, city guards and orchard watchers are valid if covered properly.
R. Hisda again: covered properly means made for shade, and any sukkah includes the rakbash sukkot.
Asks what the phrase any sukkah whatsoever is meant to include, in the ganbak list.
It includes the sukkot of the ganbak list.
The tanna of ganbak treats those sukkot as more valid because they are permanent, so he includes rakbash, which are not.
The tanna of rakbash treats those sukkot as more valid because they are obligated, so he includes ganbak, which are not.

9a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Bet Shammai rules that an old sukkah is invalid.
Bet Hillel rules that the same old sukkah is valid.
What exactly counts as an old sukkah?
Old means built thirty days before the festival; if built for the festival, it is valid even from the start of the year.
What is the reasoning behind Bet Shammai's position?
Leviticus 23:34 is cited: the festival of Sukkot is seven days to the Lord, so a sukkah must be built expressly for the festival.
Bet Hillel also seems to need that same verse; what is it used for in their case?
It serves R. Shesheth's teaching, in R. Akiba's name, that sukkah wood is forbidden for all seven days, derived from the seven-days-to-the-Lord phrase.
A baraita from R. Judah b. Batera: the sanctity of Heaven's name rests on the sukkah just as it rests on the festival offering.
The verse about seven days to the Lord is cited, and the festival is 'to the Lord' just as the sukkah is 'to the Lord'.
Does Bet Shammai also need that verse for this same deduction?
Yes, Bet Shammai also needs it for that deduction.
So what, then, is the actual reasoning of Bet Shammai?
A different verse, Deuteronomy 16:13, is cited: you shall make the festival of Sukkot for seven days.
Therefore a sukkah must be made expressly for the sake of the festival.
Bet Hillel also seems to need that verse; what does it teach them?
It teaches that one may build a sukkah on the intermediate days of the festival.
Bet Shammai follows R. Eliezer, who holds that one may not build a sukkah on the intermediate days of the festival.
But doesn't Bet Hillel hold the view that Rav Judah transmitted?
Rav Judah in Rav's name: a sukkah made of thorns, hair or thistles is invalid, but one made from tufts is valid.
When this was said before Shmuel, he objected that even a tuft-made sukkah must be invalid, since the weaving must be for its own sake.
If weaving must be for its own sake, shouldn't a sukkah also have to be made for its own sake here?
A sukkah built for its own sake is different, because that case concerns tzitzit.
Deuteronomy 22:12 says 'twisted cords you shall make for yourself', meaning for the specific purpose of your obligation.
Here too the verse says 'the festival of Sukkot you shall make for yourself', meaning for the specific purpose of your obligation.
That verse is needed to exclude a stolen sukkah; but in the tzitzit case it is also needed to exclude stolen tzitzit, so why is it not parallel?
In the tzitzit case there is a different verse, Numbers 15:38, which handles that exclusion.
Numbers 15:38 is quoted: they shall make for themselves from their own material.

9b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A sukkah built under a tree is treated as if it were built inside a house.
On a sukkah placed atop another sukkah, the upper one is valid and the lower one invalid.
R. Judah says the lower one is valid if the upper one has no occupants.
Rava limits the Mishnah to a tree whose shade exceeds the sunlight passing through it; if sunlight exceeds shade, it is valid.
How do we know this? Why does the Mishnah say as if built inside a house instead of simply saying invalid?
Rather, the phrasing teaches us something new about trees.
The tree is compared to a house: just as a house has more shade than sunlight, so a tree's shade exceeds its sunlight.
But if sunlight exceeds shade, the sukkah joins invalid covering with valid covering, which should be disqualified.
R. Papa answers that the case is one where the branches were interwoven.
If the case is interwoven branches, what is the point of the teaching?
One might have thought we should decree against interwoven covering in general; the Mishnah teaches that we do not decree.
A teaching is cited: a sukkah trained on vine, gourd or ivy and covered with valid covering is invalid, unless the valid covering predominates or the growths are cut.
To what case does that teaching refer?
If it refers to non-interwoven growths, then invalid covering is joined with valid covering, which should be disqualified.
Rather it must refer to interwoven growths; from this we learn we do not decree, and this applies only ex post facto, not ab initio.
The Gemara opens the case of a sukkah above a sukkah, citing the Mishnah.
A baraita: you shall dwell in Sukkot, not in a sukkah under another, nor under a tree, nor inside a house.
On the contrary, the plural Sukkot seems to imply two sukkot, which would permit one above another.
R. Nahman b. Isaac answers that the word is written defectively, so it does not imply two.
R. Jeremiah says: sometimes both are valid, sometimes both invalid, sometimes the lower is valid and the upper invalid, and sometimes the reverse.
In what case are both valid?
Both are valid when the lower one's sunlight exceeds its shade, the upper one's shade exceeds its sunlight, and the upper one is within twenty cubits.
Sometimes both are invalid, which Jeremiah's list also covers.
In what case are both invalid?
Both are invalid when each has more shade than sunlight and the upper one is higher than twenty cubits.
Sometimes the lower one is valid and the upper one invalid.

10a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: In what circumstances does the lower-sukkah case arise?
The lower one has more shade than sun and the upper one more sun than shade, with both within twenty cubits of the ground.
Sometimes the upper one is valid and the lower one invalid.
What is the case for this?
Both have more shade than sun, and the upper one stands within twenty cubits.
This is obvious; why state that the lower is valid and the upper invalid?
It was necessary, since one might decree invalidation to prevent joining invalid and valid covering; the Mishnah teaches it is valid.
How much space must separate the roofs of two sukkot for the lower one to be invalid?
R. Huna says a handbreadth, based on the uncleanness rule where a handbreadth square and high conveys and interposes, while less does neither.
R. Hisda and Rabbah son of R. Huna say four handbreadths, since no place of legal importance is less than four.
Shmuel says ten handbreadths.
What is the reasoning of Shmuel?
Just as validity depends on a height of ten handbreadths, so invalidity depends on ten handbreadths.
The Mishnah is cited: R. Judah says if there are no occupants in the upper one, the lower one is valid.
What does it mean that there are no occupants?
If it means actual occupants, the word occupants seems to be a determining factor, which is problematic.
Rather, no occupants means the sukkah is not fit for dwelling at all.
How so, what is the case where it is not fit for dwelling?
Where it is less than ten handbreadths high.
Does this imply that the first tanna holds that even an unfit sukkah is still invalid?
R. Dimi reports the Western view: if the lower one cannot bear the bolsters and cushions of the upper one, the lower one is valid.
Does this imply that the first tanna holds the lower one is invalid even if it cannot bear the weight?
The difference is whether the lower one can bear the weight only with difficulty.
Mishnah: spreading a sheet over the sukkah against the sun or against falling leaves, or over a four-post bed frame, invalidates it; a two-post bed frame is permitted.
R. Hisda says the ruling applies only to a sheet spread against falling leaves; spreading it for beautification is valid.
Isn't that obvious? The Mishnah says because of falling leaves.
The Mishnah's wording reflects the common practice, and the teaching is meant to inform us that beautification is also valid.
Can we say a baraita supports R. Hisda's view?
A baraita: one who covered a sukkah properly and decorated it with hangings, fruit and vials may not use those items, which supports the view that decoration is not a defect.

10b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The law runs until the end of the last day of the Festival, and if one made a condition about the decorations, everything follows that condition.
Perhaps the ruling was stated about decorations placed at the side of the sukkah.
The decorations of a sukkah do not reduce its valid size.
R. Ashi says that decorations at the side do reduce the sukkah's size.
Minyamin, R. Ashi's servant, soaked his shirt in water and spread it over their sukkah.
R. Ashi tells him to remove it, so people do not conclude that a covering susceptible to impurity is permitted.
But can they not see that it is wet?
R. Ashi means the ruling applies when the shirt is dry.
R. Nahman rules that decorations removed four handbreadths from the skhakh are valid.
R. Hisda and Rabbah son of R. Huna rule that such decorations are invalid.
R. Hisda and Rabbah son of R. Huna came to the house of the exilarch.
R. Nahman sheltered them in a sukkah whose decorations were four handbreadths from the skhakh.
They were silent and said nothing to him.
Have our rabbis retracted their teaching?
They replied that they were messengers performing a mitzvah and so were exempt from the obligation of sukkah.
R. Judah says in Shmuel's name that one may sleep in a canopied bed in a sukkah with a flat roof, provided the canopy is under ten handbreadths high.
Come and hear: one who sleeps in a canopied bed in a sukkah has not fulfilled his obligation.
Here we are dealing with a canopy that is ten handbreadths high.
It was objected: one who sleeps under the bed in a sukkah has not fulfilled his obligation.
Shmuel explained that this refers to a bed ten handbreadths high.
Come and hear: spreading a sheet over the frame of a four-post bed invalidates the sukkah.
There too the frame is ten handbreadths high.
But surely that is not how it was taught.
A baraita: two-post frames and four-post frames; a sheet over four-post frames invalidates, over two-post frames is valid.
This holds provided the two-post frames are not ten handbreadths above the bed.
Does this imply that four-post frames are invalid even when they are less than ten handbreadths high?
Four-post frames are different, since they are permanent.
But a sukkah placed above another sukkah is also permanent, and Shmuel said its validity and invalidity are equal.
Invalidating a sukkah requires ten handbreadths, while making a tent requires less; the upper case is about making a tent.
R. Tahlifa b. Avimi says in Shmuel's name that one who sleeps naked in a canopied bed may put his head out and recite the Shema.
It was objected: one who sleeps naked in a canopied bed may not put his head out to recite the Shema.
That case refers to a canopy ten handbreadths high.
This stands to reason from the final clause, which compares it to a naked man standing in a house who may not put his head out of the window to recite the Shema.

11a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: As for a house, even if it is under ten handbreadths high, it is permanent and therefore a valid tent, no worse than a four-post bed frame.
Another version: Rav Judah says in Shmuel's name that one may sleep in a bridal bed in a sukkah, since it has no roof, even if it is ten handbreadths high.
It was objected: one who sleeps in a canopied bed in a sukkah has not fulfilled his obligation.
Here we are dealing with a bed that has a roof.
A baraita: naklitin are two-pole frames and kinofot four-pole frames; a sheet over naklitin is valid if they are not ten handbreadths above the bed.
If they are ten handbreadths above the bed, is the sukkah not invalid even without a roof?
Naklitin are different because they are permanent; they are not considered permanent compared with kinofot, but are compared with a bridal bed.
Rabbah bar R. Huna expounds that one may sleep in a canopied bed even with a roof and even if it is ten handbreadths high.
This follows R. Judah, who holds that a temporary tent cannot nullify a permanent tent.
A Mishnah: R. Judah said they were accustomed to sleep under a bed in the presence of the elders.
Why not simply state that the halakha follows R. Judah?

Had it said that, one might think it applies only to a bed made for lying on, not a canopied bed, so the teaching states the reason: a temporary tent does not nullify a permanent one, whatever the bed.

Mishnah: a vine, gourd or ivy trained over the sukkah and covered with skhakh invalidates it, unless the skhakh predominates or the growths are cut; the general rule is that impure, non-ground-growing items cannot serve as skhakh.
R. Joseph sat before R. Huna and stated that if the growths were cut the sukkah is valid, and Rav says they must be shaken.
R. Huna replies that Shmuel already said this.
R. Joseph responds that Rav also said it, and Shmuel said it too, so he did not deny Shmuel's view.
R. Huna says his point was that Shmuel said it and not Rav, since Rav validates the case without shaking.
A case from R. Amram the Pious, who attached fringes to his household's aprons and did not cut the thread ends, is cited.
Rav's ruling, brought by R. Hiyya b. Ashi: the threads may be cut and they are valid.
It follows that the cutting is considered the making, so here too cutting is considered making.
Does Shmuel not hold that cutting is not considered making?
Shmuel taught in R. Hiyya's name: if one attached tzitzit to two corners at once and then cut the threads, they are valid.
Does this mean he first knotted and then cut?
No: he cut first and then knotted.
What is this teaching, and what might one have thought?

11b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: One might think the threads must be inserted one corner at a time; since that is not required, the teaching clarifies it.
It was objected: threads hung without cutting their ends are invalid.
Does this mean invalid forever, which would refute Rav?
Rav replies that invalid means invalid until the ends are cut.
Shmuel, Levi and R. Matanah in Shmuel's name hold that such threads are invalid forever.
Another version: R. Matanah says this happened to him, and Shmuel ruled that the threads are invalid forever.
It was objected: threads inserted and then cut at the ends are invalid.
A baraita on the sukkah verse, you shall make and not from what is already made, is cited regarding vines, gourds and ivy covered with skhakh, which are invalid.
To what case does this refer?
If the growths were not cut, the reason should be that they are attached to the ground, so the case must be cut growths, which are still invalid.
We learn from this that cutting is not considered making.
Is this a refutation of Rav?
Rav replies that the growths were pulled so their making is not apparent, and the ends were then cut.
The baraita where the threads were inserted and then cut is a difficulty for Rav.
Can we say this matches a dispute between tannaim?
A baraita on a lulav plucked in transgression: R. Shimon b. Yehozadak says invalid, the Sages say valid.
They thought everyone agrees a lulav must be bound, and that the lulav law is derived from the sukkah law.
Is the dispute not precisely about this principle?
The one who validates holds that cutting is making for a sukkah, and so plucking is making for a lulav; the one who invalidates denies both.
No: all agree that for a sukkah cutting is not making, and the dispute is whether the lulav law is derived from the sukkah law.
The one who validates does not derive lulav from sukkah; the one who invalidates does.
Alternatively, if a lulav must be bound, all agree the law is derived from sukkah, and the dispute is whether binding is required, matching the tannaim on lulav validity.
A baraita: a lulav, bound or unbound, is valid; R. Judah says bound is valid and unbound is invalid.
R. Judah's reason: he derives take from take, comparing the lulav to the bundle of hyssop, so it must be taken in a bundle.
The Sages do not derive take from take.
According to whom is the following taught?
Is the lulav a mitzvah to bind if it is valid unbound? If the baraita follows R. Judah, why is unbound valid; if the Sages, why a mitzvah?
It follows the Sages, and the binding is a mitzvah because of the verse this is my God and I will adorn Him.
The general rule: whatever is susceptible to ritual impurity may not be used for skhakh, whatever is not susceptible and grows from the ground may be used.
Resh Lakish derives this from Genesis 2:6, a mist rising from the earth, so the sukkah covering must be a non-impure item growing from the soil.
This works on the view that the booths were clouds of glory, but what about the view that they were real sukkot?
A baraita: R. Eliezer says the booths were clouds of glory; R. Akiva says they were real sukkot made for themselves.
That works for R. Eliezer, but what can be said for R. Akiva?
R. Dimi cites R. Yohanan: the verse you shall make the Festival of Sukkot compares the sukkah to the festival offering, so it must be made of a non-impure item growing from the soil.

12a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Just as the festival offering is a live animal, shouldn't the sukkah also be made of something alive?
Ravin cites R. Yohanan: the verse about gathering from the threshing floor and winepress refers to the waste of those.
But perhaps the verse means the actual threshing-floor and winepress produce?
R. Zera replies that the verse says winepress, and one cannot cover a sukkah with wine-press produce.
R. Yirmiyah objects: perhaps it means solidified wine from Senir, which looks like fig cakes.
R. Zera says they had the matter in hand, but R. Yirmiyah came and disrupted it.
R. Ashi replies that the verse refers to produce from the threshing floor and winepress, not the threshing floor or winepress themselves.
R. Hisda derives the rule from Nehemiah 8:15, which lists branches of olive, myrtle, palm and thick trees.
Are myrtle branches not the same as branches of thick trees?
R. Hisda: wild myrtle is for the sukkah, and branches of thick trees are for the lulav.
Mishnah: bundles of straw, wood or brushwood may not be used as skhakh, but if untied they are valid, and all are valid for walls.
R. Yaakov reports R. Yohanan's teaching on two rulings: a haystack hollowed out to make a sukkah is not a valid sukkah.
One ruling is a decree against using a storehouse, and the other is the requirement that you shall make and not from what is made.
But R. Yaakov does not know which of the two rationales applies to which case.
R. Yirmiyah proposes: let us look at what R. Hiyya b. Abba taught in R. Yohanan's name.
R. Hiyya b. Abba cites R. Yohanan: bundles are barred because a man returning from the field might leave them on his sukkah, and the Torah requires you shall make, not from what is made.
R. Yaakov had not heard R. Hiyya b. Abba's statement.
R. Ashi challenges whether the straw bundles are barred only for the storehouse reason and not for the make-not-from-what-is-made reason, and the reverse for the haystack.
R. Yohanan could reply that where the mishnah says one may not use them as skhakh, it means only ab initio, not after the fact.

12b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The invalidity of such skhakh is because of the storehouse decree, not Torah law; the other case, where the text says it is not a sukkah, means invalid even ex post facto under Torah law.
Rav Judah says in Rav's name: a sukkah covered with male arrow-shafts is valid, with female arrow-shafts invalid.
Isn't it obvious that male shafts are valid? One might have thought they are invalid because of the female ones, so the teaching clarifies they are not.
Restating Rav's ruling: a sukkah covered with female shafts is invalid.
Isn't that obvious? One might say a receptacle made to be permanently filled is not a receptacle.
The teaching clarifies that such a receptacle is still considered a receptacle for this purpose.
Rabbah bar bar Hana, citing R. Yohanan: flax stalks that were soaked and baked are invalid skhakh, natural stalks valid, intermediate stalks left undecided.
What counts as an intermediate stage of flax, and is it pounded-but-uncombed, soaked-but-unpounded, or some other state?
Rav Judah rules that fern or wormwood may be used as skhakh.
Abaye rules that fern may be used but wormwood may not, contradicting Rav Judah.
What is the reason for Abaye's ruling?

13a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gives the rationale that foul-smelling skhakh would make one want to leave the Sukkah.
Rav Hanan b. Rava rules that izma and hegeh may be used as skhakh.
Abaye disagrees: izma is permitted but hegeh is not.
Asks for the reason behind Abaye's distinction between izma and hegeh.
Their leaves fall off, so one might leave the Sukkah and depart.
Rav Gidal in Rav's name: the forked palm branch may be used as skhakh.
Explains that a natural joining does not count, and joining a thing to itself does not count either.
Rav Hisda in the name of Ravina b. Shila: forked reeds may be used as skhakh.
Repeats the principle that natural joining and self-joining are not considered joining.
A baraita teaches that reeds and forked reeds may be used as skhakh.
Asks whether plain reeds needing mention is not obvious.
The baraita means forked reeds, so the teaching is not redundant.
Rav Hisda in Ravina b. Shila's name: bitter marsh herbs can fulfill the Pesah obligation.
Objection from a baraita: hyssop is specified but not its named varieties, which contradicts the view.
Abaye replies: names changed before Torah was given count, but these herbs never changed names.
Rava replies: marror is its ordinary name, and marsh marror is named for where it grows.
Rav Hisda: one stalk is not bundling, three is, and two is the subject of the Yose and rabbis dispute.
The Mishnah on hyssop: three stalks with three buds, and Rabbi Yose's remnant rule.
Proposed inference: if remnants need only two, the outset needs two too, so three is for the proper observance.
Objection from a baraita: Rabbi Yose requires three at the outset, contradicting the proposed inference.
Reverses the assumption: three is indispensable for Yose and only proper observance for the rabbis.
Another baraita: two stalks at outset or one remnant is valid, contradicting the requirement.
Challenges the view: how can a remnant of one be invalid when it was just said to be valid?

13b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Proposes a corrected wording: the rule applies only when the outset equals the remnant, one.
Meremar: bundles of twigs made in Sura are valid skhakh, since binding them is only for counting.
R. Abba: cone-shaped willow bundles are valid once their top-knots are untied.
Objection: they are still tied at the bottom.
Rav Papa replies that the case is one where the bundles are loosened.
R. Huna b. R. Joshua: even if not loosened, a binding not made to be carried is not a binding.
Shmuel's rule: herbs used for Pesah are unfit for a Sukkah covering, but they are not an interposition and invalidate it like air space.
Asks for the reason behind Shmuel's ruling.
When they wither they crumble and fall, so they are treated as if absent.
R. Huna: one who harvests grapes for the vat does not make the stalks susceptible to uncleanliness.
Menashia b. Gada in Rav Huna's name: harvesting grain for skhakh does not make the handles susceptible.
Explains the reasoning of each position, depending on whether the harvest is for grapes or for grain.
Asks whether Menashia b. Gada's ruling is a dispute between tannaim.
A baraita on fig boughs, vine branches, straw and palm branches, with the dispute over whether the inedible part is greater.
Asks whether the dispute is really about whether the handles are susceptible to uncleanliness.
For R. Abba this is certainly a tannaitic dispute.
Asks whether the same dispute also holds for Menashia b. Gada.
Menashia replies that all agree; the case is one where the stalks were cut for food and then used for skhakh.
Asks the reason of the rabbis if the stalks were cut for food.
Proposes that the rabbis hold the original intention is annulled once one decides to use them for skhakh.
Challenges this: can an intention really be annulled in such a case?
Cites a mishnah on vessels as a source for the principle at issue.

14a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Principle: intention can make a vessel susceptible to uncleanliness, but only a physical act can remove that status.
Proposed limit: the principle covers important vessels, while handles used only as aids to eating are made susceptible by intention.
Objection from a mishnah: handles of threshed produce are insusceptible, with Yose declaring them susceptible.
Asks how the view that threshing means actual threshing can be defended in the mishnah.
Replies that in the previous case the handles were also actually threshed.
Asks what reason the others have, if they hold the same view as Yose.
Explains Yose's reason as based on R. Shimon b. Lakish: the stalks can be turned with a pitchfork.
Asks what use the stalks have in this case.
They are usable to hold the stalks by when the bundle is taken apart.
Quotes the mishnah on handles of threshed produce and Yose's view.
Presents R. Yohanan (actual threshing) and R. Elazar (untying the bundle) on the meaning of threshed.
Asks why Yose declares them susceptible on R. Yohanan's view that threshing means actual threshing.
R. Shimon b. Lakish: since one can turn them with a pitchfork.
R. Elazar: the prayers of the righteous are likened to a pitchfork, turning divine attribute from harshness to mercy.
Mishnah: skhakh may be made of wooden planks per R. Judah; R. Meir forbids; a plank four handbreadths wide is valid if one does not sleep under it.
Rav: the dispute concerns planks of four handbreadths, where Meir holds a decree against an ordinary roof applies.
Shmuel: the dispute concerns planks under four handbreadths; with four or more, all agree it is invalid.
Asks whether planks under four, even under three, would be mere sticks.
Papa explains: with four it is invalid, under three valid, and the dispute is over three to four handbreadths and the decree rationale.
Restates the mishnah on the plank four handbreadths wide as support for testing the two views.
Shmuel's view fits the mishnah: with four handbreadths it is invalid, which explains why one may not sleep under it.
Challenges Rav: why, per R. Judah, may one not sleep under a plank that is valid in his view?
Asks whether this statement is held by all.
The concluding statement agrees with R. Meir only.
Objection: a baraita states that two sheets combine.

14b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Dispute: two boards do not combine to make a valid covering, but R. Meir says boards combine like sheets.
Reads Samuel consistently: the dispute is for planks under four handbreadths, while four or more is invalid for all.
Explains combining as joining the planks to make four handbreadths.
Asks how Rav's reading works: with four handbreadths why combine, and without four why is it invalid?
Explains: there are four handbreadths, and they combine to form four cubits at the side.
Another version of the same explanation, consistent with Samuel's position.
Asks what combining means in the other version.
On Rav's reading, the question is how R. Judah can say the covering is valid even with four handbreadths.
Asks what it means to say they do not combine, since they would be mere sticks.
Since R. Meir said they combine, R. Judah in turn said they do not combine.
Notes that the teaching is in agreement with both Rav and Samuel.
Baraita on cedar planks: under four is valid; with four R. Meir invalidates and R. Judah validates.
R. Judah's anecdote: in a time of danger they covered a balcony with four-handbreadth planks and sat under them.
Objection: a time of danger is no proof for the law.
Baraita on the Shmuel reading, with concessions from R. Meir on spacing and from R. Judah on sleeping under a four-handbreadth plank.
Rav Huna holds that planks placed on their sides are invalid; Rav Hisda and Rabbah b. Rav Huna hold valid.
Rav Nahman in Sura rules such planks on their sides are invalid, like metal spits.
Rav Huna rebukes the students for not saying his way.
The students object that the Master never gave them a reason they could accept.
Rav Huna replies: you never asked me for a reason, and I would have given it.
Proposes a supporting baraita: a sukkah must contain the head, body and table, and a plank four handbreadths wide with only three inside is invalid.
Asks whether the case is one where the planks are placed on their sides.
No: the case is a plank over the entrance with three handbreadths inside and one outside, which counts as part of the Sukkah.

15a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: an unplastered wooden roof; Judah, Shammai, Hillel and Meir differ on loosening or removing planks.
Explains Bet Hillel's reasoning: the verse requires making, and loosening or removing a plank counts as an action.
Asks what the reason of Bet Shammai is.
Asks whether, on the ordinary roofing decree, one act should suffice.
Indeed it is the decree against ordinary roofing, and Shammai says so even if one loosens the planks.
If one removes one plank from between two, it is valid; otherwise it is not.
Asks: if so, read the concluding part of the Mishnah.
Cites Meir's ruling: remove one from between two, but do not loosen.
Proposes that Meir is in fact Bet Shammai's view, and Bet Shammai and Bet Hillel did not dispute this point.
Asks what the Mishnah then teaches us.
Meir holds a decree against looking like ordinary roofing; Judah holds there is no such decree.
Objects: they already disputed this, as the mishnah on planks shows, with Judah permitting and Meir forbidding.
R. Hiyya b. Abba in R. Yohanan's name: the earlier mishnah deals with planed boards, forbidden as a decree against vessels.
Challenges with Rav Judah's ruling on arrow-shafts: no decree against plain shafts because of bored ones.
Asks why they would dispute the same question twice in the two mishnayot.
Meir replies that Bet Shammai and Bet Hillel do not dispute the matter at all.
