Asks what practical difference lies between these two formulations.
The difference shows with an inflated skin used as a wall: invalid under the wind version, valid under the human-made version.

24b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Completes the earlier point: a partition built by human hands is valid.
The Master cites Rabbi Yose the Galilean: a get may not be written on such material.
Asks the reason for Rabbi Yose the Galilean's view.
A baraita: the word scroll teaches that a get may be written on any material lacking the breath of life.
The Rabbis object: if the verse said in a scroll the view would fit, but 'a scroll' refers to the recital of words.
Asks how the Rabbis interpret the words 'and he wrote'.
They teach that divorce takes effect by writing, not money, lest one think exit parallels entry, which is by money.
Asks how Rabbi Yose the Galilean derives this principle.
He derives it from the scroll of divorce: the scroll alone severs; other Sages need that wording for a different purpose.
A baraita: a conditional get that lasts forever does not sever, while one limited to thirty days does.
Mishnah: one who builds a Sukkah between trees, which form its walls, is valid.
Rav Aha b. Jacob: a partition that cannot withstand a normal wind is not a valid partition.
The Mishnah's case: a Sukkah between trees, with the trees forming its walls, is valid.
Objects: the trees sway back and forth, so how can they serve as valid walls?
Replies that the case is one where the branches were plaited with shrubs and bay branches.
Asks what the Mishnah then teaches, if that case is already resolved.
One might decree against it lest a person use the tree; so the Mishnah teaches that it is valid.
Brings a baraita on a tree, fence or reed partition as a valid corner; the same plaiting explanation applies.
Objects: if plaiting resolves the sway, carrying beneath the tree should be permitted throughout its whole area.
Objects, citing Rav Huna son of Rav Joshua, who forbids carrying objects beneath such a tree at all.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A principle: an abode serving the open air permits carrying only within two beth se'ah.
A baraita about a raised or sunken Shabbat resting place seems to contradict the principle.
Mishnah: those on a mitzvah errand, the sick and their attendants are exempt from the sukkah.
Asks the source for the exemption, citing the verse about sitting in your house and walking on the road.
A baraita derives exemptions from the verse, excluding one occupied with a mitzvah and a groom, and the bridegroom rule.
Asks what the verse's implication is for the exemption.
Rav Huna: the road parallels other non-obligatory activity, excluding one occupied with a mitzvah.
Objects that the case concerns a mitzvah journey, so the verse should simply say sitting and going.
Asks what the words sitting and going add, if the verse were read that way.
Going for one's own purposes is obligated; going on a mitzvah is exempt.
If so, one who marries a widow should also be exempt, and the same logic applies to a maiden.
A maiden-bringer is preoccupied, while a widow-bringer is not, so the distinction holds.
Anyone preoccupied should be exempt, so one losing a ship at sea should also be exempt.
Rav Abba bar Zavda quotes Rav: mourners are obligated in all mitzvot except tefillin, which are called splendor.
Preoccupation with a mitzvah differs from preoccupation with a non-obligatory matter, so the rule stands.
Asks whether the exemption for one occupied with a mitzvah is derived from the earlier verse.
It is derived from the other verse, not the earlier one.
A baraita on Numbers 9:6 about the impure men who carried Joseph's bones, per Rabbi Yose HaGlili.

25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Akiva says Mishael and Elzaphan were occupied with the bodies of Nadav and Avihu.
R. Yitzchak objects: if they carried Joseph's coffin they could have purified themselves, and so could Mishael and Elzaphan.
Rather, they were occupied with a met mitzvah whose seventh day fell on the eve of Pesach.
Numbers 9:6 says they could not keep the Passover on that day, but could the next day.
Both teachings are needed: one covers Pesach timing, the other covers Shema where karet is or is not involved.
R. Abba bar Zavda in Rav's name: a mourner is obligated in all Torah mitzvot except tefillin.
Tefillin are called beauty, as in Ezekiel 24:17, so the mourner is obligated in them but others are exempt.
This applies only to the first day of mourning, as Amos 8:10 describes that day as bitter.
R. Abba bar Zavda in Rav's name: a mourner is obligated in the sukkah.
Asks whether this is not obvious.
If one in discomfort is exempt from the sukkah, then the mourner, also in discomfort, should be exempt too.
Only discomfort that comes on its own exempts; a mourner causes his own discomfort and must settle his mind.
R. Abba bar Zavda in Rav's name: the groom, groomsmen and wedding guests are exempt from the sukkah for all seven days.
Asks what the reason for this exemption is.
They must rejoice, and rejoicing happens only under the huppah and at a place of meal.
Then they should make the huppah itself inside the sukkah.
Abaye says the reason is seclusion; Rava says it is the groom's discomfort.
Asks what the practical difference between these two reasons is.
Where people go in and out, the seclusion reason gives no restriction, while the discomfort reason does.
R. Zera: he ate in the sukkah and rejoiced under the huppah, fulfilling two mitzvot.
A baraita: the groom and wedding guests are exempt from prayer and tefillin but obligated in Shema.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: In R. Shila's name: the groom is exempt from the sukkah, while the groomsmen and wedding guests are liable.
A baraita of R. Hanania ben Akavya exempts holy-work craftsmen, supporting R. Yose HaGalili that one doing a mitzvah is exempt from other mitzvot.
A baraita exempts day, night and mitzvah travelers from the sukkah in the stated periods, illustrated by R. Hisda and Rabbah's night sleep.
A baraita sets the exemption for town watchmen by day and by night, with the opposite obligation in the other period.
Watchmen of gardens and orchards are exempt both by day and by night.
If so, they could build a sukkah there and dwell in it.
Abaye: the verse says you shall dwell, meaning as you normally dwell, so a temporary shelter does not count.
Rava: a breach calls out to the thief, so the watchman is exposed to theft in the garden.
Asks what the practical difference between the two reasons is.
The difference appears when the watchmen guard a pile of fruit.
The mishnah exempts the sick and their attendants from the sukkah.
A baraita says the sick include one with mild illness, like eye or head pain, supported by Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's case.
Precedents where Rav and Rava permitted sleeping outside the sukkah, for gnats or a plaster smell.
Rava holds consistently that one in discomfort is exempt from the sukkah.
But the mishnah teaches the sick and their attendants are exempt, not merely those in discomfort.
The sick person and his attendants are exempt, while one merely in discomfort is exempt but not his attendants.
Casual eating and drinking are permitted outside the sukkah.
Asks how much eating counts as casual.
R. Joseph: two or three eggs' worth.
Abaye objects that this amount can suffice for a full meal, which would make it a set meal.
Rather, Abaye: as much as a student eats before entering the learning session.
A baraita: casual eating is permitted outside the sukkah, but casual sleeping is not.
Asks the reason for prohibiting casual sleep outside the sukkah.
R. Ashi: it is a decree, lest one fall into deep sleep.
Abaye objects with a baraita permitting casual sleep in tefillin, asking whether one should fear falling asleep.
R. Yosef bar Ila'i: the baraita refers to one who entrusts his sleep to others.
R. Mesharsheya raises a difficulty from the proverb that your guarantor needs a guarantor.
Rabbah bar bar Hana in R. Yohanan's name: the case is one who places his head between his knees.
Rava: there is no set amount of sleep that counts as regular.
A baraita: one may sleep casually in tefillin but not regular sleep.
Two further baraitas conflict with the first, one allowing both casual and regular sleep, the other neither.
No conflict: one case has tefillin held in hand, one on the head, and one under a cloth.
Asks how long casual sleep lasts.
Rami bar Yehezkel: the time it takes to walk one hundred cubits.
A baraita says one who sleeps in tefillin and sees a seminal emission removes them by holding the strap.

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yaakov says one should not hold the tefillin box; the Sages permit casual sleep in tefillin but not regular sleep.
Asks how long casual sleep lasts.
The time it takes to walk one hundred cubits.
Rav: sleeping by day is forbidden beyond the amount of a horse's sleep.
Asks what the sleep of a horse amounts to.
Sixty breaths.
Abaye says the Master sleeps as Rav did, and Abaye himself slept as long as a walk from Pumbedita to Be Kube.
Rav Yosef applies Proverbs 6:9 to Abaye's long daytime sleep, rebuking him as a sluggard.
A baraita on whether one who sleeps by day may keep tefillin on, and R. Yose's view on children who must always remove them.
Does R. Yose hold that one with a seminal emission may not wear tefillin?
Abaye: the case is young men with their wives, lest they become accustomed to the practice.
A baraita on one who forgot and had intercourse while wearing tefillin, who must wash his hands before removing them.
Mishnah: the sages were served food and water in the sukkah, and R. Zadok ate less than an egg's bulk outside it without a blessing.
Does this case come to contradict the mishnah's ruling?
Rather, the mishnah is missing a clause allowing one to be strict on oneself, and the case is then consistent.

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The story repeats: Rabbi Zadok ate less than an egg's bulk outside the sukkah, without washing or blessing.
Does this case refute R. Joseph and Abaye, who require a sukkah for an egg's bulk? Perhaps smaller amounts need no washing or blessing.
R. Eliezer requires fourteen sukkah meals, one by day and one by night, while the Sages set no number beyond the first night.
Asks the reason for R. Eliezer's position.
Dwelling in a sukkah is like dwelling in a house, so one eats there when one wants, and the rabbis read the verse this way.
If so, the first festival night should also not be obligatory.
R. Yohanan in R. Shimon ben Yehozadak's name: the first night is obligatory like the first night of Pesach matzah.
Asks how we know that the first night of Pesach is obligatory.
Exodus 12:18, at evening you shall eat matzah, shows Scripture set the first night as an obligation.
R. Eliezer said fourteen meals in the sukkah are required, contradicting his later concession.
Bira in R. Ammi's name: R. Eliezer changed his mind.
Asks how one makes up a missed first-night meal.
If made up with bread, one is only eating the day's regular meal.
Rather one makes up with various desserts, and a baraita confirms that this fulfills the obligation.
Agrippa's steward asks whether a man who eats only one meal a day can fulfill his obligation with one sukkah meal.
R. Eliezer: you extend your own meal with many appetizers for honor, so why not add one for your Creator?
Asks whether one who has two wives and two sukkahs may move from one sukkah to the other to fulfill the obligation.
No: one who moves from one sukkah to another annuls the mitzvah of the first.
A baraita introduces R. Eliezer's view.

27b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Sages and R. Eliezer dispute moving between sukkot and building one on Hol HaMoed; both agree a fallen sukkah may be rebuilt then.
Asks the reason for R. Eliezer's position.
R. Eliezer: the verse requires a sukkah fit for the full seven days.
The Rabbis read the verse as requiring a sukkah for the festival, so rebuilding on Hol HaMoed is permitted.
Asks whether this is not obvious, or whether one might think it is a different sukkah not meant for seven days.
The ruling teaches that it is indeed not obligated for seven days.
A baraita: just as one cannot fulfill the lulav obligation with a neighbor's lulav, one cannot use a neighbor's sukkah, per Lev. 23:40 and Deut. 16:13.
The Sages: one may fulfill the sukkah obligation in a neighbor's sukkah, since all Israel are fit to dwell in one sukkah, per Lev. 23:42.
Asks what the Rabbis derive from the words for yourself.
It excludes a stolen sukkah, while a borrowed one is covered by all homeborn.
Asks what R. Eliezer derives from all homeborn.
It includes a convert or minor who became eligible during the festival.
The Rabbis need no verse, since building on Hol HaMoed is already established by their ruling.
A story: R. Ila'i went to greet his teacher R. Eliezer in Lod on the festival.
Ila'i challenges R. Eliezer's praise of those who stay home, citing R. Yitzchak's derivation that one must greet a master on the festival.
No difficulty: greeting is required when one can go and return the same day, but not when one cannot.
A story: R. Eliezer spent Shabbat in a sukkah in Caesarea and the sun reached it.
Asks whether he may spread a cloth over the sukkah to block the sun.
Every tribe produced a judge, so the judge's authority supports the request.
The sun reached the middle of the sukkah.
Asks again whether he may spread a cloth over it.
Every tribe produced a prophet, and Judah and Benjamin appointed kings through prophets.
The sun reached R. Eliezer's feet, R. Yohanan spread a cloth, and R. Eliezer left the sukkah.
He did not leave to evade the answer, but because he never said what he had not heard from his master.
How could R. Eliezer have acted this way, given his ruling that one may not move between sukkot?
That occurred on another festival.
But he also praised those who stay home on festivals.
That occurred on Shabbat.
Could the case be settled from his own statement instead?
A Mishnah on window shutters: R. Eliezer and the Sages dispute shutting a window on Shabbat with a fastened shutter.

28a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara distinguishes the cases: where the item annuls the matter it is forbidden, where it does not annul it, it is permitted.
A baraita: R. Eliezer was asked thirty sukkah laws, knowing twelve and not eighteen, while R. Yose son of R. Yehudah reverses the counts.
They tell R. Eliezer that all his words are merely hearsay from tradition.
R. Eliezer replies that they forced him to say what he had not heard from his teachers, and he never spoke unheard teaching.
Praise of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and of R. Eliezer, his student, for never speaking untraditional words or wasting time in the House of Study.
A baraita on Hillel's eighty disciples, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's breadth of knowledge, and Yonatan ben Uziel's Torah study.
Mishnah: if one's head and most of his body are in the sukkah but his table is indoors, Bet Shammai invalidate it and Bet Hillel validate it.
Bet Hillel cite the elders of both houses who visited Rabbi Yohanan ben HaHoroni and did not object to his sitting that way.
Bet Shammai reply that this is no proof, and the elders retort that such a custom means one never fulfilled the sukkah obligation.
Mishnah: women, slaves and minors are exempt from the sukkah, while a minor no longer dependent on his mother is obligated.
The story of Shammai the Elder's daughter-in-law, who had a minor's bed covered with skhakh so the child could use the sukkah.
Asks the source for the rule, as the Rabbis taught.
A baraita: the word homeborn excludes women, while the word every includes minors.
The Gemara's objection: a baraita says the homeborn includes women, a conflicting reading of the same word.
Rabbah: these are traditional laws, and the Rabbis attached them to a verse as a mnemonic.
Asks which rule is verse-based and which tradition, and why a verse is needed for a time-bound positive commandment women are exempt from.
Yom Kippur's rule about women is derived from Rav Yehudah's teaching in Rav's name.
The school of R. Ishmael taught that Numbers 5:6, man or woman, supports including women in the rule.

28b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the verse equates women with men for all Torah punishments.
Abaye replies that the sukkah law is a received halakhic tradition, not derived from the verse.
Lest one infer from the dwelling verse that the sukkah must mirror a home, which would include the wife.
A permanent home is shared by husband and wife, so the sukkah would be too; the verse teaches the opposite point.
Rava says the verse is necessary and gives his own reason.
Hypothesis: the sukkah might be derived from the matzah law of the fifteenth, where women are obligated.
A gezerah shavah on the word fifteenth links the sukkah obligation to the matzah festival.
The matzah analogy is kept to teach a specific point about women's status under the sukkah law.
If the sukkah is a tradition, why does the verse exist at all?
The verse serves to include converts among those obligated.
Lest one restrict the obligation to the native-born, citing the Leviticus verse about the native in Israel.
The phrase native-born does not exclude converts; the verse makes this explicit.
Is the Yom Kippur obligation for women derived from Rav Judah's teaching in Rav's name?
No; the verse is needed to add the extra affliction, not to derive the obligation.
Since the Torah excluded the extra affliction from punishment and warning, women might be wholly exempt.
Therefore the verse teaches that women are in fact obligated to fast.
The master says the word all includes minors in the sukkah obligation.
A mishnah lists women, slaves and minors as exempt from the sukkah, seemingly contradicting that.
No conflict: one source concerns a trained minor, the other a minor not yet trained.
Is a trained minor's obligation only rabbinic rather than Torah-based?
Yes; the verse is merely a support (asmakhta) for a rabbinic obligation.
Quotes the mishnah phrase about a minor who no longer needs his mother.
What does a minor who no longer needs his mother look like in practice?
The school of R. Yannai: one whose mother no longer needs to wipe him after relieving himself.
R. Shimon says: one who wakes from sleep and does not call out to his mother.
Older people also call their mother, so this criterion seems inadequate.
Rather the text should read the child calling out for his mother upon waking.
Introduces a case in which a daughter-in-law gave birth in Shammai's household.
Was the case cited to contradict the earlier halakhah?
Something is missing from the text; it should be read with Shammai's stricter stance.
Shammai is stricter; in the case he opened the roof plaster and laid skhakh over the bed for the infant.
Mishnah: the sukkah is the permanent home for the festival; rain permits leaving once porridge spoils, illustrated by a parable.
Tanna'im teach the rule and its example: good vessels, bedding, eating, drinking and leisure in the sukkah.
What is the source of this teaching of the tanna'im?
Leviticus 23:42, you shall dwell as you ordinarily dwell, is cited as the source.
The rule is restated: sukkah as permanent home, with vessels, bedding, eating, and study in the sukkah.
Objection: doesn't Rava rule about where Scripture and Mishnah should be studied?
Rava's ruling: Scripture and Mishnah are studied in the sukkah but recited outside it.
No conflict: one case concerns recitation, the other examination of the text.

29a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Narrative: Rava and Rami b. Hama before R. Hisda first reviewed the gemara together, then reasoned out the grounds.
Rava rules which vessels may stay in the sukkah: drinking vessels, not eating vessels, pitchers, pails and lamps.
Others report a different version of Rava's ruling on the lamp and the vessels.
No real disagreement: one ruling concerns a large sukkah and the other a small one.
Introduces the mishnah case of rain falling, citing the baraita on bean porridge spoiling.
Narrative: Abaye sits before R. Joseph in a sukkah when wind drops twigs into the food; Joseph orders the vessels moved.
Abaye objects by citing the mishnah that the porridge must be spoiled before one may leave.
Joseph replies that, being delicate, his own spoiling point comes when he is disturbed by the twigs.
Baraita: one eating in the sukkah when rain falls need not be moved until the meal is finished; likewise sleepers until dawn.
Is the sleeper's limit until he wakes, or until dawn light appears?
Come and hear: the baraita says until light appears, which supports dawn.
Objection: the baraita says until dawn appears too, so both readings seem to be stated.
Rather the text should read until he wakes and then dawn appears, reconciling both.
Introduces a parable.
Who spilled on whom: did the servant pour on the master or the reverse?
Comes a baraita where a master poured a pitcher over his servant's face and refused his service, as a precedent.
Baraita: a solar eclipse is a bad omen for the world, compared to a king who removes a lamp from servants and leaves them in the dark.
R. Meir: lunar and solar eclipses are bad omens for Israel's enemies, compared to a teacher with a strap and a child used to beatings.
Baraita: eclipses signify different things for idolaters, Israel, eastern and western regions, and the whole world.
An eclipse with red or sackcloth-like color signals sword or famine; its timing at sunset or dawn determines when calamity comes.
Some say the order of these signs is reversed.
Every nation's gods are struck together with it, so when a nation is punished, its gods suffer too.
Cited from Exodus 12:12: I will execute judgments against all the gods of Egypt.
When Israel does God's will, they need not fear these omens.
Cited from Jeremiah 10:2: do not learn the ways of the nations or fear heavenly signs; idolaters fear them, Israel does not.
Baraita: four causes of a solar eclipse: an Av Bet Din dying without proper eulogy, a betrothed girl crying unaided, sodomy, and two brothers killed together.
Four causes of lunar and luminary eclipses: forgers, false witnesses, raising small livestock in Israel, and cutting down good trees.
Four causes for householders' property being handed to government: keeping paid bills, and lending with interest.

29b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continues the list: those able to protest but who did not, and those who publicly pledge charity but never give.
Rav's four causes for householders' property being confiscated: withholding or stealing wages, removing the yoke onto others, and arrogance.
Contrast with the humble: Psalm 37:11 says the humble will inherit the land and delight in peace.
Chapter closing formula, then the mishnah on invalid lulavim: stolen, dry, from an idolatrous tree or a wayward city, or with a cut top or detached leaves.
R. Yehuda says a lulav with a cut top may be tied from above, and Iron Mountain fronds are valid.
A lulav must have three handbreadths of frond to be waved, and then it is valid.
The gemara says the mishnah states the law clearly, with no difference between the first and second day of the festival.
Granted a dry lulav needs to be beautiful, but which case does the stolen lulav cover?
On the first day the stolen case is excluded by the verse 'for you', meaning your own property.
But on the second day, why would a stolen lulav not be excluded?
Resolution attributed to R. Yochanan in the name of R. Shimon b. Yochai.

30a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The stolen animal is disqualified because the owner's act of bringing it is a mitzvah fulfilled through a transgression.
Malachi 1:13 mentions bringing a stolen animal, compared to the lame one, which cannot be fixed; ownership by despair makes no difference.
Before despair the verse says from you, which excludes the stolen animal; after despair it becomes his, so why is it still invalid?
Despair does transfer ownership, so the disqualification must be because the mitzvah is fulfilled through a transgression.
Attribution: R. Yochanan cites R. Shimon b. Yochai on the matter.
Isaiah 61:8 says God loves justice and hates robbery in a burnt offering.
Parable: a king orders his servants to pay the toll though the whole toll is his, so travelers learn not to evade it; so too God hates theft in offerings.
R. Ami: a dry lulav is invalid for lack of beauty, and a stolen one because the mitzvah is fulfilled through transgression.
R. Yitzchak disagrees, quoting Shmuel that the stolen lulav is invalid only on the first day, and Rav Nachman objects from a borrowed lulav.
When would a borrowed lulav count as valid? If the first day, the verse says from your own, so the case must be the second day.
Rava: the mishnah applies on the first day, with no need to state the borrowed case; a stolen lulav is ownerless by despair, so it is treated as his.
Rav Huna tells merchants to have non-Jews cut the hadasim, because idolaters are land robbers and their property is stolen.

30b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Land cannot be stolen, a principle that the Gemara treats as a basis for the solution.
Therefore have the merchants cut the hadasim, so despair happens in their hands and the change of ownership in yours.
Objection: if merchants cut them, the change of ownership would still occur in the buyer's hands, so the solution is unnecessary.
Not needed: the case concerns the hadasim the merchants themselves cut.
Could they not acquire the hadasim through a change made by action, such as tying them into the bundle?
The reasoning is that R. Huna held a lulav does not require a tie.
Even if a lulav needs a tie, a change that returns to its original form does not count as a change.
Could they not acquire them through a change of name, since they were called asa before and now are called otherwise?

31a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Originally the name asa was also used alongside hoshana, so a name change does not settle the acquisition question.
Baraita: a sukkah that is stolen, or roofed with schach taken from public property, is invalid per R. Eliezer and valid per the Sages.
Rav Nachman explains the dispute about removing a fellow from his sukkah, and R. Eliezer's view that one cannot fulfill the mitzvah in another's sukkah.
The Sages' view: one can fulfill the mitzvah in a fellow's sukkah, since land cannot be stolen, so it is a borrowed sukkah.
If one stole wood and built a sukkah, all agree he owes only the value of the wood.
From where do we learn that a stolen sukkah refers to Rav Nachman's interpretation?
The baraita compares it to public property: as there the land is not his, so the sukkah's land is not his.
Narrative: an old woman came to Rav Nachman, complaining that the exilarch and his court sat in a sukkah built with her stolen wood, but he ignored her shouting.
The woman objects that she is a descendant of Abraham with many servants, and Rav Nachman still pays her no attention.
Rav Nachman rules that she is a chatterbox and is entitled only to the value of the wood.
Ravina compares this to a sukkah beam, where the Sages fix a remedy from the old statute on beams built into houses.
Is this obvious, and how does it differ from ordinary wood?
Wood is commonly found but beams are not, so the law is needed to state that beams follow the same rule.
Within the seven days one returns the beam itself, but after the festival the value; if the beam is plastered in, the value is owed at once.
Baraita: a dried lulav is invalid, but R. Yehuda validates it.
Rava explains the dispute: the Sages compare the lulav to the etrog and so require beauty for the lulav, while R. Yehuda does not compare them, though all require beauty for the etrog.
Does R. Yehuda not require beauty for the lulav, since the mishnah says he ties the fronds from above?
No: his reason is that the palm fronds were split and must be tied, not that beauty is required.
But the mishnah says we bind a lulav only with its own species, per R. Yehuda, so the reason must be beauty?
No; Rava said one may bind even with vines or palm bark, which are not beautiful.
Rather R. Yehuda's reason is that a lulav needs binding, and using another species would make five species.
For the etrog, does R. Yehuda really require beauty?
Baraita: the four species may not be added to or subtracted from; without an etrog, one brings no substitute; wilted ones are valid but dried ones are invalid.
R. Yehuda holds that even dried ones are valid, and he adds that an event once happened to illustrate it.

31b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Describes city-dwellers who bequeathed their lulavs to descendants, cited as support for using dried lulavs.
The Sages object: that practice was a time of distress, which is no valid proof.
Still, it is taught that R. Yehuda validates even dried ones.
Does this not refer to the etrog?
No, it refers to the lulav.
Mishnah: just as one may not subtract from the four species, one may not add to them.
Why state this, since it is obvious, unless one might think a lulav bundle needing a tie allows adding another species?
The ruling teaches that adding another species is not allowed.
Mishnah: if no etrog is found, one may not bring a pomegranate, quince, or anything else in its place.
Why state this, since it is obvious, unless one might bring a substitute so the etrog law is not forgotten?

Explains the Evil Inclination's stench and its attack on Israel, and Abaye glosses it as targeting scholars most

The old man's teaching: the greater the man, the greater his inclination

Cites Genesis 6:5 about the inclination of man's heart being evil all the time

ranges.en: R. Shimon b. Lakish: a person's evil inclination grows stronger daily and seeks to kill him
Cites Psalms 37:32-33: the wicked watches the righteous, but God does not leave him to it
School of R. Ishmael: if this wretch meets you, drag him to the study house, where stone and iron are softened and broken
Cites Isaiah 55:1, Job 14:19 and Jeremiah 23:29 for the images of water wearing stone and fire breaking rock
R. Shmuel b. Nahmani, citing R. Yohanan: the inclination entices a man in this world and testifies against him in the next

R. Huna asks why Hosea says the spirit of harlotry leads astray and also says it is within them
Rava: first it is called a passer-by, then a guest, and finally a man, so the difference is in its stages
Cites II Samuel 12:4 where the traveller, guest and man are successive stages in the parable
R. Yohanan: there is a small organ in man, which is satisfied when starved and starved when satisfied
Cites Hosea 13:6 about being fed and becoming full
R. Hana b. Aha: the Holy One regrets creating four things: exile, Chaldeans, Ishmaelites and the Evil Inclination

Cites Job 12:6 on the tents of robbers prospering, for the Ishmaelites

Asks who the four craftsmen in Zechariah 2:3 are
R. Hana b. Bizna, citing R. Shimon Hasida: Messiah son of David, Messiah son of Joseph, Elijah and the Righteous Priest

Dismisses the argument: why should he argue with Hana in matters of aggada
Cites Micah 5:4 on seven shepherds and eight princes, and identifies each of them by name
Baraita: the lamp was fifty cubits high, and four priestly youths carried jars of oil totalling 120 log

Baraita: the Temple's youths surpassed the son of Martha bat Boethus, who was forbidden to carry the cut of an ox
Cites Proverbs 14:28 that in a multitude of people is the glory of the king
Asks in what respect these youths were superior

Closing remark: there was no courtyard in Jerusalem, and a baraita is introduced

ranges.en: Mishnah: a woman sifted wheat by the light of the Beit Hashoevah, and the pious men and men of deeds were there
Baraita: some say happy is our youth that did not shame our old age, others say happy is our old age that atoned for youth
Hillel the Elder rejoiced at the water-drawing festival and said that where he goes, his feet lead him, and God comes to him
Cites Exodus 20:21 that God will come to the one in every place where His name is mentioned and bless him
A skull that drowned others is itself drowned, and R. Yohanan says a man's feet lead him where he is wanted
Introduces the two Cushites who attended on Solomon

Objects that R. Elazar taught never to reproach Heaven, so Levi's lameness had some other cause
Explains that Levi's lameness had both causes, the reproach and the kidah
Levi juggled eight knives before Rabbi, Shmuel eight glasses before Shapur, and Abaye eight or four eggs before Rabbah

Ahitophel replies that it is permitted, and David writes the Name on a sherd
Story: the sherd is cast into the Deep, which subsides and then rises, and Ulla and Mesharsheya draw lessons about the earth
Mishnah quoted: the priests stood at the upper gate that descends
R. Jeremiah asks whether the tenth step means descending five and standing on ten, or the reverse, and the question stands
Baraita argues from Ezekiel 8:16 that the faces toward the east must mean the backs were toward the Temple
Explains the phrase as teaching that they uncovered themselves and defecated facing the Temple
Quotes the cry, we are the Lord's and our eyes are turned to the Lord, as an alternative version of the Shema
Objects from R. Zera that reciting Shema twice is like saying Modim twice, so this cry should not be said
Explains that the people worshipped eastward and then gave thanks, so the wording was about worship not thanks
Mishnah sets the number of trumpet blasts in the Temple each day, on Shabbat and during Sukkot
Explains that the Mishnah does not follow R. Judah, citing his baraita on the minimum and maximum blasts
Asks what the two sides dispute

Asks the reason for R. Judah's view
Cites Numbers 10:5 with utekatem teruah and yitka'u teruah as the basis for R. Judah
Asks how this works out in practice
Concludes that tekiah and teruah count as one blast according to R. Judah

Asks what the Rabbis' reason is

Asks whether it is obvious that this follows R. Judah

Mishnah reference: on the eve of Shabbat during the intermediate days of the festival
Asks why the tenth step is not mentioned in the Mishnah, and whose view it follows
Identifies the view as R. Eliezer b. Jacob, citing a baraita that he sounds three blasts at the altar
Whoever says three on the tenth step omits the altar, and whoever says the altar omits the tenth step
Asks what the reasoning of R. Eliezer b. Jacob is
R. Eliezer holds the altar is preferable since the gate blast already covers the tenth step, while the Rabbis hold the reverse
R. Aha b. Hanina arrives from the south with a baraita on the trumpets of the priests
Cites Numbers 10:8 and 10:10, deriving that the blasts follow the number of additional offerings
Mishnah: on the eve of Shabbat during the festival there were forty-eight blasts
Asks why the Mishnah does not state fifty-one blasts for Shabbat during the festival

Rava rejects that explanation, noting the teaching is given daily, and the count lets the reader infer both views
Rava's alternative: no blast for the Water-Drawing on Shabbat, so the total is much lower
Asks why the Mishnah does not also teach Rosh Hashanah falling on Shabbat, which has three additional offerings
The Mishnah needed to teach the eve of Shabbat during the festival to establish R. Eliezer b. Jacob's view
Objects that the Tanna should not be asked why he taught one case rather than another, since both could have been taught
Asks what the Tanna omitted, given that he taught some cases and left others out
He omitted the eve of Pesach

Objects that the Mishnah's forty-eight limit is contradicted by the eve of Pesach falling on Shabbat, which has fifty-one or fifty-seven blasts

When the first festival day falls on the eve of Shabbat, it is postponed, so that Yom Kippur is not on a Sunday
Objects that the Mishnah teaches that Shabbat fats are offered on Yom Kippur, so postponement is not needed
R. Zera describes the teaching on Yom Kippur falling before or after Shabbat, and the view of R. Judah b. R. Shimon b. Pazzi
There is no difficulty, since one ruling is that of the Rabbis and the other that of the Others
Baraita of the Others: the gap between Shavuot or Rosh Hashanah in successive years is at most four weekdays, or five in a leap year
Objection from a baraita: if Rosh Hodesh falls on Shabbat its psalm supersedes the Shabbat psalm, so both should be read
R. Safra explains supersedes as meaning recited first, since the frequent takes precedence over the less frequent
R. Yohanan: the Rosh Hodesh offering is a sign that the new month was fixed at its proper time
Objects that other distinguishing signs are used for the offerings, so the sign cannot be the reason
Cites the baraita on where the morning tamid, additional and Rosh Hodesh offering fats were placed on the altar

ranges.en: R. Yohanan's explanation continues: two distinguishing signs were made so that different people would see one or the other
Objects with a baraita that the blast should be sounded separately for each additional offering, as for Shabbat and Rosh Hodesh
Scripture says and on your New Moons, which settles the matter
This is a refutation of R. Aha
Abaye: the verse compares all months with one another, since they are all sanctified alike
R. Ashi: the month of Rosh Hashanah has two beginnings yet is called one month, so the verse counts it as one
Introduces a baraita on what was recited on each day of Hol Hamoed
Lists the Psalms recited on each of the six days of Hol Hamoed, citing Psalms 29, 50, 94, 81 and 82
If Shabbat falls on one of these days, the psalm that begins with the earth being moved is set aside
R. Safra and R. Papa give mnemonics for the order of the psalms of the days
Notes that this is a refutation of R. Aha b. Hanina
Objects that R. Aha b. Hanina himself cited both a verse and a baraita in support of his view
Ravina explains the blasts are lengthened, while the Rabbis of Caesarea in R. Aha's name say the number of trumpeters increases
Asks how we proceed when we keep two days of the festival
Abaye rules the second day's paragraph is omitted; Rava rules the seventh day's is omitted
A baraita agrees with Rava: if Shabbat falls on one of these days, the psalm that begins with the earth being moved is set aside
Amemar instituted in Nehardea that they repeat the previous portions

ranges.en: Mishnah: on the first festival day thirteen bulls, two rams and one goat were offered, and six watches each offered two lambs

Asks whether the Mishnah follows Rabbi rather than the Rabbis
Baraita: for the bull offered on the eighth day, lots are cast at first, according to Rabbi
The Sages hold that one of the two watches that did not share in bulls offers it
Replies that the Mishnah can agree with the Rabbis, since two watches still need lots
Asks whose view is followed by the baraita on watches repeating a second and third time
Replies that the baraita may follow the Rabbis, and explains the point of the third-time rule
The Mishnah's rule: one who offered bulls on one day may not offer them the next, but all take turns
R. Eliezer: the seventy bulls of the festival correspond to the seventy nations
The single bull of the eighth day corresponds to the unique nation of Israel
Parable: a king asks his servants for a great feast, then a simple meal with his beloved friend, to explain the eighth day
R. Yohanan: woe to the idolaters, for the altar once atoned for them and now nothing atones
Mishnah: at three festivals all watches share equally in the festival offerings and in the showbread
Asks whether the festival emurim are not the Most High's portion
R. Hisda: the emurim are what is said to be for the festival, so they are shared by the watches
Baraita derives from Deuteronomy 18:6 and the single gate that all watches share equally in festival emurim

Asks how one knows that all watches share equally in the division of the showbread

ranges.en: Derives from Deuteronomy 18:8 that the equal portions to eat refer to the showbread, not to sacrifices
Exposition of the exception for what the fathers sold: each takes his week in turn

Asks whether Rav and Rabbah b. Bar Hannah dispute on the same principles as Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
Baraita on the points of dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel over the blessing of the day and of the wine at a meal, with reasons

Mishnah: when a festival falls next to Shabbat, all watches share the showbread, with differing loaf counts for each watch

Asks what before and after mean, if before is the first day and after the last
Before means the last day of the festival and after means the first day, so the watches can meet early and leave late
The Rabbis enacted this so that the watches could eat together, since some arrive early and some leave late
Mishnah: if one day intervened between the festival and Shabbat

ranges.en: Asks what function these two extra watch portions served

Reasoning on the view that the late watch is penalized: this makes sense as a reason to penalize the whole watch

Closing formula marking the end of the chapter and of Masekhet Sukkah
